## Etymology

[edit]

The word "west" is a Germanic word passed into some Romance languages (ouest in French, oest in Catalan, ovest in Italian, vest in Romanian, oeste in Spanish and Portuguese). As in other languages, the word formation stems from the fact that west is the direction of the setting sun in the evening: 'west' derives from the Indo-European root \wes reduced from \wes-pero 'evening, night', cognate with Ancient Greek ἕσπερος hesperos 'evening; evening star; western' and Latin vesper 'evening; west'. Examples of the same formation in other languages include Latin occidens 'west' from occidō 'to go down, to set' and Hebrew מַעֲרָב (maarav) 'west' from עֶרֶב (erev) 'evening'.

West is sometimes abbreviated as W.

## Navigation

[edit] [...] ## Symbolic meanings

[edit]

In Chinese Buddhism, the West represents movement toward the Buddha "Buddha (general)") or enlightenment (see Journey to the West). The ancient Aztecs believed that the West was the realm of the great goddess of water, mist, and maize. In Ancient Egypt, the West was considered to be the portal to the netherworld, and is the cardinal direction regarded in connection with death, though not always with a negative connotation. Ancient Egyptians also believed that the Goddess Amunet was a personification of the West. The Celts believed that beyond the western sea off the edges of all maps lay the Otherworld, or Afterlife. **West** is one of the four cardinal directions or [points of the compass](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Points_of_the_compass "Points of the compass"). It is the opposite direction from [east](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East "East") and is the direction in which the [Sun sets](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sunset "Sunset") on the [Earth](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earth "Earth").

## Etymology

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=West&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Etymology")]

The word "west" is a [Germanic](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Germanic_languages "Germanic languages") word passed into some [Romance languages](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romance_languages "Romance languages") (*ouest* in French, *oest* in Catalan, *ovest* in Italian, *vest* in Romanian, *oeste* in Spanish and Portuguese). As in other languages, the word formation stems from the fact that west is the direction of the setting sun in the evening: 'west' derives from the Indo-European root *\*wes* reduced from *\*wes-pero* 'evening, night', cognate with Ancient Greek ἕσπερος [hesperos](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hesperus "Hesperus") 'evening; evening star; western' and Latin vesper 'evening; west'.[[1]](#cite_note-1) Examples of the same formation in other languages include Latin [occidens](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Occident "Occident") 'west' from occidō 'to go down, to set' and Hebrew מַעֲרָב (maarav) 'west' from עֶרֶב (erev) 'evening'.

West is sometimes abbreviated as **W**.

## Navigation

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=West&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Navigation")]

To go west using a compass for [navigation](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Navigation "Navigation") (in a place where magnetic north is the same direction as true north) one needs to set a [bearing](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bearing_(navigation) "Bearing (navigation)") or [azimuth](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Azimuth "Azimuth") of 270°.

West is the direction opposite that of the [Earth](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earth "Earth")'s rotation on its axis, and is therefore the general direction towards which the [Sun](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sun "Sun") appears to constantly progress and eventually set. This is not true on the planet [Venus](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Venus "Venus"), which rotates in the opposite direction from the Earth ([retrograde rotation](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Retrograde_and_prograde_motion "Retrograde and prograde motion")). To an observer on the surface of Venus, the Sun would rise in [the west](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poles_of_astronomical_bodies "Poles of astronomical bodies") and set in the east[[2]](#cite_note-compare-2) although Venus's opaque clouds prevent observing the Sun from the planet's surface.[[3]](#cite_note-3)

In a map with north at the top, west is on the left.

Moving continuously west is following a [circle of latitude](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Circle_of_latitude "Circle of latitude").

## Weather

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=West&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Weather")]

Due to the direction of the Earth's rotation, the prevailing wind in many places in the [middle latitudes](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Middle_latitudes "Middle latitudes") (i.e. between 35 and 65 degrees [latitude](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latitude "Latitude")) is from the west, known as the [westerlies](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Westerlies "Westerlies").[[4]](#cite_note-Glossary_of_Meteorology_2009-4)[[5]](#cite_note-Sue_Ferguson-5)

## Cultural

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=West&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Cultural")]

Further information: [Western culture](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_culture "Western culture")

The phrase "the West" is often spoken in reference to the [Western world](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_world "Western world"), which includes the [European Union](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Union "European Union") (also the [EFTA](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Free_Trade_Association "European Free Trade Association") countries), the United Kingdom, the Americas, Israel, Australia, New Zealand and (in part) South Africa.

The concept of the Western part of the earth has its roots in the [Western Roman Empire](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_Roman_Empire "Western Roman Empire") and the [Western Christianity](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_Christianity "Western Christianity"). During the [Cold War](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cold_War "Cold War") "the West" was often used to refer to the [NATO](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NATO "NATO") camp as opposed to the [Warsaw Pact](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warsaw_Pact "Warsaw Pact") and [non-aligned nations](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Non-Aligned_Movement "Non-Aligned Movement"). The expression survives, with an increasingly ambiguous meaning.

## Symbolic meanings

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=West&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Symbolic meanings")]

In [Chinese Buddhism](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinese_Buddhism "Chinese Buddhism"), the West represents movement toward the [Buddha](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buddha_(general) "Buddha (general)") or enlightenment (see [Journey to the West](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Journey_to_the_West "Journey to the West")). The ancient [Aztecs](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aztec "Aztec") believed that the West was the realm of the great goddess of [water](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Water "Water"), mist, and [maize](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maize "Maize"). In [Ancient Egypt](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ancient_Egypt "Ancient Egypt"), the West was considered to be the portal to the [netherworld](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underworld "Underworld"), and is the cardinal direction regarded in connection with [death](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Death "Death"), though not always with a negative connotation. Ancient Egyptians also believed that the [Goddess](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goddess "Goddess") [Amunet](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amunet "Amunet") was a personification of the West.[[6]](#cite_note-6) The [Celts](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celt "Celt") believed that beyond the western sea off the edges of all maps lay the [Otherworld](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Otherworld "Otherworld"), or Afterlife.

In [Judaism](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Judaism "Judaism"), west is seen to be toward the [Shekinah](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shekinah "Shekinah") (presence) of God, as in Jewish history the [Tabernacle](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tabernacle "Tabernacle") and subsequent [Jerusalem Temple](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jerusalem_Temple "Jerusalem Temple") faced east, with God's Presence in the [Holy of Holies](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holy_of_Holies "Holy of Holies") up the steps to the west. According to the [Bible](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bible "Bible"), the [Israelites](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israelites "Israelites") crossed the [Jordan River](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jordan_River "Jordan River") westward into the [Promised Land](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Promised_Land "Promised Land").

In [Islam](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Islam "Islam"), cardinal directions carry spiritual significance, but the emphasis is often on the [omnipresence](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Omnipresence "Omnipresence") of God rather than symbolic geography. The West, like all directions, is encompassed by the divine presence. The [Qur’an](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quran "Quran") states: "To God belong the East and the West. Wheresoever you turn, there is the Face of God. God is All-Encompassing, All-Knowing." (2:115). This verse underscores the idea that spiritual truth transcends direction, offering a contrast to traditions that attach specific symbolic meanings to the West.

In [American literature](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_literature "American literature") (e.g., in *[The Great Gatsby](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Great_Gatsby "The Great Gatsby")*) moving West has sometimes symbolized gaining [freedom](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liberty "Liberty"), perhaps as an association with the settling of the [Wild West](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wild_West "Wild West") (see also the [American frontier](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_frontier "American frontier") and [Manifest Destiny](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manifest_Destiny "Manifest Destiny")).
